lead: Today the Church sets aside the purple of Lent for white and keeps the solemnity of St Joseph, the husband of Mary. All the readings follow one promise on its way. God tells David through Nathan that an heir of his will have a throne forever. St Paul recalls Abraham, who believed a promise when all appearances were against it. Matthew shows both promises reaching their goal through a man of David’s line who says nothing and does what he is told. Today’s psalm sings of the same promise to David.
The Gospel may be either Matthew or Luke 2:41–51a; a note on Luke is among the questions below. The key words are house, hoping against hope and righteous.

set: David is king in Jerusalem and has brought the ark there (2 Samuel 6). Settled in his house of cedar, he wants to build a house for God, since “the ark of God stays in a tent” (7:2). The prophet Nathan approves at first, but that night the word of the Lord comes to him.

This oracle is the foundation of Israel’s hope for a son of David. The word “covenant” does not appear in this chapter, but Psalm 89, today’s psalm, uses it: “I have made a covenant with my chosen one” (89:3).
str: vv. 4–5a: God’s word comes to Nathan: are you the one to build me a house?
vv. 12–13: David’s heir: his kingdom and his throne.
v. 16: David’s house, kingdom and throne, forever.
¶ The Lectionary omits vv. 5b–11, where God recalls what he has done for David, and vv. 14b–15, where he promises that even if the heir sins, his steadfast love will not depart.
kw: The whole chapter plays on this one word. It can mean a palace (David’s), a temple (the one he plans) and a dynasty (what God promises). David offers God a house; God says “the Lord will make you a house” (7:11).
Literally “seed”. It first points to Solomon, who will build the Temple (1 Kings 6), and it opens out toward a son beyond him.
From the same root as our word Amen: firm, reliable. The future of David’s house rests on God’s fidelity, not on the conduct of its kings.
vv: Are you the one to build me a house to live in?
David’s idea is generous, but God will not be housed by a king’s plan. The first move in this story, as in every story of grace, is God’s.
I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your body, and I will establish his kingdom.
The promise looks beyond David’s death. He will not live to see what is promised, a thing he shares with Abraham.
I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me.
A king of Israel was called God’s son by adoption. Hebrews 1:5 applies this verse to Christ, in whom it is true in a way no king of Judah could have dreamed.
Your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me; your throne shall be established forever.
Solomon’s kingdom split, and the last king of Judah went into exile. Israel went on hoping because this word still stood. Psalm 89 itself shows the pain of that waiting.
ch: The angel says to Mary: “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his ancestor David” (Luke 1:32). The Catechism says that God called Joseph to take Mary as his wife so that Jesus should be born into the messianic lineage of David (CCC 437), and that many recognized in Jesus the promised son of David (CCC 439). Joseph holds no throne. He is a workman in a small town, and through him the line is handed on. Jesus also speaks of the true house of God, “the temple of his body” (John 2:21).

set: St Paul writes to the Christians of Rome, probably around AD 57, before going to Jerusalem and hoping to reach them. In chapters 1–4 he argues that Jews and Gentiles alike are made right with God by grace through faith in Christ. Abraham is his great witness, since Genesis says he believed and God “reckoned it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6), before circumcision and long before the law given at Sinai.
Paul does not despise the law: “we uphold the law” (3:31). His point is about where the promise comes from.
str: v. 13: the promise came through the righteousness of faith.
vv. 16–17: it rests on grace, for all Abraham’s descendants, in the presence of the God who gives life.
kw: What God binds himself to do. A promise can only be received and trusted. This is Paul’s key word in the chapter.
Literally “beyond hope, in hope”. All human reasons for hoping have gone, and Abraham hopes because of God.

A word from accounting: to enter to someone’s account. Paul is quoting Genesis 15:6. For the Catholic understanding, God’s reckoning is not merely a legal entry: justification truly makes us just and renews us within (CCC 1987–1989).
vv: For the promise that he would inherit the world did not come to Abraham or to his descendants through the law but through the righteousness of faith.
Genesis promised Abraham a land and many nations. Paul widens it to “the world”: all peoples are to share in the blessing.
in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his descendants,
If it rested on our record, it would never be secure. Because it rests on grace, it holds.
who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.
The God of Abraham’s faith is the Creator and the God of resurrection. This is what makes hope possible when things look finished.
Hoping against hope, he believed that he would become “the father of many nations,”
The verse fits Joseph as well. In the dark, with no explanation that anyone could check, he trusted what God said.
Therefore his faith “was reckoned to him as righteousness.”
The Lectionary ends here, and Matthew’s Gospel then calls Joseph righteous (Matthew 1:19). The word links the two.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham shows what faith is (CCC 146), and that Christian hope has its origin and model in his (CCC 1819). St John Paul II wrote in Redemptoris Custos that Joseph was the first to share in the faith of the Mother of God (5). Faith, as Paul says elsewhere, works “through love” (Galatians 5:6), and by grace our deeds truly bear fruit (CCC 2008–2010). Joseph’s faith, like Abraham’s, lives in what he does.

r.h: He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him
set: Matthew’s Gospel opens with the genealogy of Jesus, “the son of David, the son of Abraham” (1:1), and each line runs “the father of”. At v. 16 the pattern breaks: Joseph is “the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born”. In Greek “of whom” is feminine. So the genealogy leaves a question: how does Jesus belong to David’s line if Joseph is not his natural father? Vv. 18–25 give the answer.

Background. Betrothal in that time was a binding bond. The couple were already called husband and wife, and it could be ended only by a formal divorce, but the woman often stayed in her family home for a time before moving to her husband’s house. It is in this interval that Mary is found to be with child.
str: v. 16: the end of the genealogy.
v. 18: Mary is with child “from the Holy Spirit”.
vv. 20–21: the angel in a dream: do not be afraid; name him.
¶ This is the first of four dreams in which God directs Joseph (1:20; 2:13; 2:19; 2:22). The Gospels do not record a single word he said.
kw: In Matthew, one who lives by God’s will as the law teaches it. His righteousness shows here in his care both for God’s law and for Mary’s name.
The usual word for ending a marriage or a betrothal by divorce. “Quietly” probably means with the fewest possible witnesses, without a public charge.

The Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, from the name Yehoshua, “the Lord saves” (CCC 430). The father gave the name. By naming the child, Joseph takes him legally as his son, and so Jesus becomes, in law, a son of David.
vv: and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.
Matthew chooses his words with care: Jesus is born of Mary, and Joseph’s place is that of her husband.
Her husband Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.

The Fathers read this in more than one way. St Jerome says that Joseph, knowing Mary’s purity, kept silent about a mystery he did not understand (in substance). St Bernard says that in reverence he felt unworthy to stay near so great a mystery (in substance). Others think he believed that she had sinned and yet would not shame her. On every reading he is merciful.
Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

Elsewhere in Matthew “son of David” is said of Jesus alone. The title reminds Joseph who he is and why he is needed. The Catechism says that the angel’s words teach the virginal conception, a divine work beyond all human understanding (CCC 497).
She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.
Joseph is given a task, not an explanation of everything. The name says what the child will do.
he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him;
This is Joseph’s whole answer: he gets up and does it. St John Paul II calls this the “obedience of faith” in Joseph (Redemptoris Custos 4, in substance).
ch: St Augustine defended the marriage of Mary and Joseph as a true marriage, and Joseph as truly a father to Jesus, though not by the flesh (in substance). Pius IX declared him patron of the universal Church in 1870, and Pope Francis marked the 150th anniversary with the letter Patris Corde (2020), which speaks of him as a father in the shadows, working, accepting and creatively courageous. The Catechism commends us to St Joseph as patron of a happy death (CCC 1014).

qa: Did Mary and Joseph have other children? Verse 25 says “until”.

The Greek word for “until” says what happened up to a point, not what happened afterward. The Church confesses Mary’s perpetual virginity (CCC 499). The “brothers” of Jesus in the Gospels are understood as close relatives; the word could have that wider sense in Semitic usage (CCC 500).
What does Joseph teach us if he never speaks?

That holiness does not depend on being heard. His whole witness is doing what God asks, at once and in the dark, for the sake of those in his care. Countless fathers and workers, whose lives no one will ever write about, can see themselves in him.
What of the other Gospel, Luke 2:41–51a?

There Jesus, aged twelve, stays behind in the Temple. Mary says, “your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety” (2:48), and Jesus speaks of his Father’s house. Then “he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them” (2:51). So the Son of God learned as a boy to obey this man, in the home he provided (CCC 532, 534).
rite: In the Roman calendar this is a solemnity: the Gloria and the Creed are said at Mass even in Lent. This year it falls on a Friday, and the Church’s law does not bind us to Friday abstinence when a solemnity falls on that day (Code of Canon Law, canon 1251). St Joseph’s name has stood in the Roman Canon since St John XXIII added it in 1962, and it was added to the other Eucharistic Prayers in 2013. Many Catholics keep March as St Joseph’s month. Two days from now Holy Week begins, and we can ask him, who protected the child from those who sought his life, to stay with us as we walk beside the Son at the Passion.
study: David wanted to do something great for God, and God said he would do it himself. What am I trying to build by myself that I should let God build?
Joseph acted without having the full picture. What is the next plain thing God is asking of me, even if I do not see where it leads?
Paul says the promise rests on grace. Where do I still act as if it rests on my record?
Who are the people in my care whom I protect, as Joseph did, without being noticed? How can I honor those who do this for me?
